{{Short description|Mathematical method}}
{{More sources|date=August 2024}}

The '''Petrov–Galerkin method''' is a mathematical method used to approximate solutions of [[partial differential equations]] which contain terms with [[Even and odd numbers|odd]] order and where the test function and solution function belong to different function spaces.<ref>J. N. Reddy: ''An introduction to the finite element method'', 2006, Mcgraw–Hill</ref> It can be viewed as an extension of [[Galerkin method|Bubnov-Galerkin method]] where the bases of test functions and solution functions are the same. In an operator formulation of the differential equation, Petrov–Galerkin method can be viewed as applying a projection that is not necessarily orthogonal, in contrast to [[Galerkin method|Bubnov-Galerkin method]].

It is named after the Soviet scientists [[Georgy Petrov|Georgy I. Petrov]] and [[Boris Galerkin|Boris G. Galerkin]].<ref name="Birthday">"Georgii Ivanovich Petrov (on his 100th birthday)", Fluid Dynamics, May 2012, Volume 47, Issue 3, pp 289-291, DOI 10.1134/S0015462812030015</ref>

==Introduction with an abstract problem==
Petrov-Galerkin's method is a natural extension of [[Galerkin method]] and can be similarly introduced as follows.

===A problem in weak formulation===
Let us consider an abstract problem posed as a [[weak formulation]] on a pair of [[Hilbert spaces]] <math>V</math> and <math>W</math>, namely,
: find <math>u\in V</math> such that <math>a(u,w) = f(w)</math> for all <math>w\in W</math>.

Here, <math>a(\cdot,\cdot)</math> is a [[bilinear map]] and <math>f</math> is a bounded linear functional on <math>W</math>.

===Petrov-Galerkin dimension reduction===
Choose subspaces <math>V_n \subset V</math> of dimension ''n'' and <math>W_m \subset W</math> of dimension ''m'' and solve the projected problem:
: Find <math>v_n\in V_n</math> such that <math>a(v_n,w_m) = f(w_m)</math> for all <math>w_m\in W_m</math>.

We notice that the equation has remained unchanged and only the spaces have changed. Reducing the problem to a finite-dimensional vector subspace allows us to numerically compute <math> v_n </math> as a finite [[linear combination]] of the basis vectors in <math> V_n </math>.

===Petrov-Galerkin generalized orthogonality===
The key property of the Petrov-Galerkin approach is that the error is in some sense "orthogonal" to the chosen subspaces. Since  <math>W_m \subset W</math>, we can use <math>w_m</math> as a [[test vector]] in the original equation. Subtracting the two, we get the relation for the error, <math>\epsilon_n = v-v_n</math> which is the error between the solution of the original problem, <math>v</math>, and the solution of the Galerkin equation, <math>v_n</math>, as follows

:<math> a(\epsilon_n, w_m) = a(v,w_m) - a(v_n, w_m) = f(w_m) - f(w_m) = 0</math> for all <math>w_m\in W_m</math>.

===Matrix form===
Since the aim of the approximation is producing a [[system of linear equations|linear system of equations]], we build its matrix form, which can be used to compute the solution algorithmically.

Let <math>v^1, v^2,\ldots, v^n</math> be a [[basis (linear algebra)|basis]] for <math>V_n</math> and <math>w^1, w^2,\ldots, w^m</math> be a [[basis (linear algebra)|basis]] for <math>W_m</math>. Then, it is sufficient to use these in turn for testing the Galerkin equation, i.e.: find <math>v_n \in V_n</math> such that

:<math>a(v_n, w^j) = f(w^j) \quad j=1,\ldots, m.</math>

We expand <math>v_n</math> with respect to the solution basis, <math>v_n = \sum_{i=1}^n x^i v^i</math> and insert it into the equation above, to obtain

:<math>a\left(\sum_{i=1}^n x^i v^i,\, w^j\right) = \sum_{i=1}^n x^i a(v^i, w^j) = f(w^j) \quad j=1,\ldots,m.</math>

This previous equation is actually a linear system of equations <math>A^Tx=b</math>, where

:<math>A_{ij} \stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=} a(v^i, w^j), \qquad\text{and}\qquad b_j \stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=} f(w^j).</math>

====Symmetry of the matrix====
Due to the definition of the matrix entries, the matrix <math>A</math> is [[symmetric matrix|symmetric]] if <math>V=W</math>, the bilinear form <math>a(\cdot,\cdot)</math> is symmetric, <math>n=m</math>, <math>V_n=W_m</math>, and <math>v^i=w^j</math> for all <math>i=j=1,\ldots, n=m.</math> In contrast to the case of [[Galerkin method|Bubnov-Galerkin]] method, the system matrix <math>A</math> is not even square, if <math>n\neq m.</math>
